summary: Mobility is approaching pre‑pandemic levels with an MF‑Index of 72 and PT ridership at 1.29 million trips daily, yet actual fuel savings from the work‑from‑home mandate remain negligible. High‑risk sectors continue to show very high mobility scores, signalling exposure to fuel price volatility and congestion.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 million litres saved per week contrasts sharply with the measured 334,000 litres (≈1% of target) in the first week, indicating poor compliance and limited real‑world fuel‑saving impact.
Daily PT trips of 1.29 million translate to ~471 million trips annually, roughly 10% below the 2019 level but a clear rebound from the MCO trough, suggesting recovery momentum.

Logistics, construction and retail sectors record mobility scores of 85‑95 despite high fuel prices (RON95 RM3.47/L), exposing the economy to cost‑inflation and congestion risks if price pressures persist.
WFH adoption is uneven: public/GLC employees at 60% versus retail (15%), logistics (8%) and construction (5%). This disparity creates unequal exposure to fuel costs and limits the mandate’s fairness.

Elevated fuel prices and a perfect fuel‑policy score create incentives for a modal shift to public transport, but PT ridership remains below pre‑pandemic levels, indicating the shift is not yet fully realized.

recommendation: Introduce tiered PT subsidies to lift daily ridership to 1.4 million trips within six months and set a concrete fuel‑saving target of 5% of the theoretical ceiling (≈1.8 million litres/week) by Q2 2027. Expand mandatory WFH incentives for high‑mobility sectors and consider a modest fuel surcharge rebate for low‑emission vehicle adoption to mitigate economic risk.
